questions.question: Explain why black women opposed the extension of pass laws in the 1950s.
questions.expected_answer: 1913 Bloemfontein women's anti-pass campaign (Charlotte Maxeke) succeeded. 1952 Abolition of Passes Act provided for women's reference books, issued from 1956. Fears: influx control could remove women from towns and separate families; arrests leaving children alone; loss of income from domestic work, trading, brewing; harassment seen with men. Double oppression: race and gender (legal minors under customary/common law).

questions.question: Describe FEDSAW and the events of the Women's March of 9 August 1956.
questions.expected_answer: ANC Women's League 1948; FEDSAW founded 17 April 1954 (about 150 delegates representing 230 000 women; Ray Alexander, Ngoyi, Joseph, Amina Cachalia, Florence Mkhize, Frances Baard); non-racial, part of Congress Alliance; Women's Charter (vote, equal pay, property, marriage rights, end racial discrimination). October 1955 march of about 2 000. 9 August 1956: about 20 000 women of all races at Union Buildings; government obstruction; leaders Ngoyi, Joseph, Moosa, Williams delivered petitions (over 100 000 signatures) to absent PM Strijdom; 30 minutes silence, fists raised; song "Strijdom, wathint' abafazi, wathint' imbokodo, uzakufa". Passes continued (Zeerust 1957), compulsory by 1963; significance: discipline, unity, women's leadership; National Women's Day, Women's Month.

questions.question: Describe the lives and roles of Lilian Ngoyi and Helen Joseph in resistance to apartheid.
questions.expected_answer: Ngoyi: born Pretoria 1911; garment worker and union leader; joined ANC in Defiance Campaign; ANC Women's League president; first woman on ANC NEC 1956; FEDSAW president; travelled abroad 1955; Treason trialist; detained 1960 (largely solitary); banned from 1962, confined to Orlando, sewing; died 1980. Joseph: born England 1905; came to SA 1931; wartime welfare officer; social worker; Congress of Democrats founder; FEDSAW national secretary; Treason trialist (acquitted 1961); first person under house arrest 1962 (Sabotage Act); harassment, assassination attempts; documented banished people; died 1992. Both worked across racial lines.
